title: Deborah, Barak and Jael Defeat Sisera
overview: When a Canaanite king oppresses Israel, the prophet Deborah sends Barak into battle, and the enemy general Sisera dies at the hands of a woman named Jael.

parts.label: Oppressed by Jabin (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: After their leader Ehud dies, Israel turns from the LORD, and the writer says God "sold" them, meaning he let them fall under the power of Jabin, a king ruling from Hazor in the north. Sisera, his general, had 900 chariots fitted with iron, a force Israel could not match, and he treated them cruelly for twenty years until they cried out for help.

parts.label: Deborah calls Barak (vv. 4-10)
parts.note: Deborah is a prophet who settles disputes under a palm tree, and she passes on God's command for Barak to gather 10,000 men at Mount Tabor. Barak will go only if she comes, which some read as fear and others as wanting a prophet's backing to rally the troops, and she warns that the LORD will hand Sisera over to a woman.

parts.label: Heber the Kenite (v. 11)
parts.note: This aside sets up the ending: Heber came from a clan related by marriage to Moses, but he had moved away and his family was at peace with King Jabin. That alliance is why Sisera will later trust his tent.

parts.label: The battle at the Kishon (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: Barak's troops leave the safety of the mountain and charge the chariots on the plain, and the LORD throws Sisera's army into panic. The song in the next chapter says the Kishon River swept the enemy away, which many take to mean a flood bogged down the chariots, and Sisera abandons his chariot to run on foot.

parts.label: Jael kills Sisera (vv. 17-22)
parts.note: In that culture, welcoming someone into your tent and feeding them was a strong promise of safety, so Jael's warm welcome and milk made Sisera feel secure. She then kills him in his sleep with a tent peg, fulfilling Deborah's words about a woman, though readers have long argued whether her act was heroic or a betrayal of trust.

parts.label: Jabin's power broken (vv. 23-24)
parts.note: The writer credits God with the victory. Israel keeps pressing until Jabin is destroyed, ending this period of oppression.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the story approves of Jael's deception and killing as a heroic act, or simply records how God brought about victory through a deed that was morally troubling.
think: When a story celebrates someone for an act that also broke trust, how do you decide whether to call them a hero?
